title: Component service lifetime with memoryless property
scenario_markdown: The operational lifetime $X$ of an industrial sensor before failure follows an exponential distribution with rate $\lambda = 0.5$ failures per thousand hours ($X \sim \text{Exp}(0.5)$). Find the probability that a sensor survives at least 3 thousand hours.
assumptions: Constant failure rate across operating lifetime

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: E[X] = 1/lambda = 2.0 thousand hours. P(X >= 3) = exp(-0.5 * 3) = exp(-1.5) = 0.22313. Memoryless property: P(X > 5 | X > 2) = P(X > 3) = exp(-1.5).

stages.prompt_markdown: Given failure rate $\lambda = 0.5$ per thousand hours, what is the expected (mean) lifetime $E[X]$ of a sensor?

options.hint_markdown: The parameter $\lambda$ is the failure rate; mean lifetime is the reciprocal $1/\lambda$.
The quantity $1/\lambda^2$ is the variance $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, not the mean.

stages.explanation_markdown: For an exponential distribution, the expected value is the reciprocal of the rate: $E[X] = 1/\lambda = 1/0.5 = 2.0$ thousand hours.

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the probability that the sensor survives at least 3 thousand hours: $P(X \ge 3) = e^{-\lambda x} = e^{-0.5 \times 3}$. Enter as a decimal rounded to at least three places.

Suppose a sensor has already operated without failure for 2 thousand hours. What is the conditional probability that it operates for at least 3 *additional* thousand hours (i.e. reaches at least 5 thousand hours total)?

options.text_markdown: $P(X > 5 \mid X > 2) = P(X > 3) = e^{-1.5} \approx 0.2231$ due to the memoryless property
Lower than 0.2231 because the sensor has accumulated 2 thousand hours of wear
options.hint_markdown: The exponential distribution possesses the memoryless property: past operational time does not affect remaining lifetime.
Conditional probability is $P(A \cap B)/P(B) = P(X > 5)/P(X > 2) = e^{-2.5}/e^{-1.0} = e^{-1.5}$.

stages.explanation_markdown: The exponential distribution is uniquely memoryless among continuous distributions: $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = \frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t} = P(X > t)$.
